title: HTTP Deep Dive
description: Master HTTP methods, headers, status codes, and the evolution from HTTP/1.1 through HTTP/2 multiplexing to HTTP/3 QUIC.

segments.text: HTTP is the language of the web. Every time your browser loads a page, fetches an API, or downloads an image, it's speaking HTTP. Let's break apart this protocol piece by piece.

HTTP methods define what you want to do. GET retrieves data. POST creates something new. PUT replaces an entire resource. PATCH updates part of it. DELETE removes it. Each verb has a clear semantic meaning.

Headers carry metadata with every request and response. Content-Type tells the server what format you're sending. Authorization carries your credentials. Cache-Control dictates caching behavior. Headers are the silent workhorses of HTTP.

Status codes are the server's answer in a number. Two hundred means success. Three-oh-one means moved permanently. Four-oh-four means not found. Five hundred means the server broke. Learn the families and you'll read any API response instantly.
Here's a question I love asking in interviews. What's the difference between a four-oh-one and a four-oh-three?
segments.thought_prompt: 401 Unauthorized vs 403 Forbidden — what's the actual difference?

segments.text: Four-oh-one means 'I don't know who you are — authenticate yourself.' Four-oh-three means 'I know exactly who you are, and you're not allowed.' Authentication versus authorization. Subtle but critical.
HTTP/1.1 has a major bottleneck — head-of-line blocking. Each connection can handle only one request at a time. Browsers open six parallel connections per domain as a workaround, but that's wasteful.

HTTP/2 fixes this with multiplexing. One single TCP connection carries many requests and responses simultaneously, interleaved as binary frames. No more head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer. Pages load dramatically faster.

HTTP/2 also brings header compression and server push. Headers that repeat across requests get compressed into tiny references. Server push lets the server send resources before the browser even asks for them.

But HTTP/2 still runs on TCP, and TCP itself has head-of-line blocking. One lost packet stalls everything. HTTP/3 ditches TCP entirely and uses QUIC — built on UDP with built-in encryption and independent streams.

QUIC establishes connections in zero round trips for repeat visitors. Zero. Compare that to TCP's one-RTT handshake plus TLS's additional handshake. The speed improvement is massive on mobile networks.
segments.thought_prompt: Why would zero-RTT connection setup matter more on mobile networks than on desktop?

segments.text: From methods and status codes to multiplexing and QUIC, HTTP has evolved from a simple text protocol to a high-performance binary machine. Understanding these layers gives you superpowers when debugging production issues.
